about: Fragments of the world's records (Docs/Design/54-gathering-places.md, 7), shown one at a time to a wolf who finishes archive work: its archive's region first, then the shared ones. `after` names a fragment that must be read first. Hand-written first set (2026-10-08), for review: dates are 'the old count', never the game's calendar.

fragments.text: Ridgemere's first record is not a charter but a fishing tally: three families, one boat, and a stretch of the Sound 'too deep to find the bottom, though we tried with all our rope tied end to end.' The town grew around the wharf before it grew around anything else.

A child's question, written down by a patient clerk: 'If the Sound has no bottom, where do the fish sleep?' Below it the clerk's answer: 'In the Sound.' Below that, in another hand and much later: 'Still the best answer anyone has given.'

A clerk's tally of dry days, kept for a whole year in the old count and then abandoned. The column for each month holds a few strokes at most. The last entry reads: 'Stopped counting. It is easier to count the other kind, and there is no point counting those either.'

The first roofer's bill for the Rain Hall, unpaid. Beneath it the Council of Houses' ruling on who should pay: each House agreeing that one of the others should. The bill has been copied forward into every new ledger since, and is still marked 'outstanding'.

An order for buckets 'for the use of the Council', placed every autumn for as long as the records go back. The number grows by one or two each year. Somebody has added it up in the margin and written: 'At this rate the Hall will be all buckets by the time anyone mends the roof.'

The Council of Houses' seating, drawn on a scrap: four chairs round a table, Greatly's nearest the fire, Grayrock's nearest the door. A note explains that Grayrock asked for the door 'so that a lord who is always leaving may leave without fuss.' The note is unsigned and very old.

Why the lowest quarter is called the Sump: every drain in the city runs downhill, and so, the record says, does everything else. A later hand has written beside it the names of the families who first built there, and a still later hand has added: 'They were not asked to.'

A storm off the Sound took the roofs from half the Commons in one night. The record names who took in whom: two long columns, almost equal, as if the clerk had wanted to show that every house that lost a roof also opened a door.
The wharf has been rebuilt six times, each recorded with the same words, 'longer this time', and a length. The lengths, put side by side, show the wharf has never once been longer than the first one.

Frosthollow's record of the deep winters: the years the valley road closed, each marked with how many days until it opened again. The longest is written in a shaking hand, and under it a list of who shared their lamp oil.
The first miners' rule, still read aloud at the pithead: nobody goes down alone, and nobody comes up without counting the others. Below it, scratched in later: 'Count twice.'
A fisher's note on Glasswater: so clear on a still day that you can watch your own line sink, and so cold that 'a wolf who falls in has time to be surprised, and not much else.'

Why Coldwater keeps the old saying that the Long River is 'borrowed water': it leaves Glasswater here and does not come back. The clerk who wrote it down adds that Coldwater has been trying to send a bill downriver ever since.

A woodcutter's custom, written down at Oakhaven: for every oak felled in the Warmwood, an acorn planted. The tally of trees felled and acorns planted runs for many pages. The acorns are always ahead, by a little.

A list of the fen paths around Mirebridge, each with a note: 'safe in summer', 'safe if dry', 'safe if you know it'. The last few just say 'do not'. Someone has added a path at the bottom with no note at all, and nobody has dared to ask whose hand it is.

Larkfield's oldest market rule: a stall goes to whoever is there first on market day, and the first one there must sweep it. The records show a long run of very early, very clean market days, and then a year when nobody came before noon.

Southmeadow's harvest book: every year's grain and every year's apples, side by side. In the good years the clerk draws a small sun in the margin. In the bad years, a small apple, so that at least the page has one.

A scholar's note on the calendar: the old count began 'when the packs first agreed on which day was which', and the scholar suspects this took longer than a day. Several early years are recorded twice, once by each of the packs who disagreed.

An old list of the touched: wolves who could warm a den with a breath, find water under stone, or mend a bone faster than it broke. Beside each, two words in the same careful hand: 'Gifted' or 'Quickened'. No record says who first drew the line between them, or why.

A healer's record: the Gifted, she writes, are like a good fire, and towns gather round them. The Quickened are like a fire too, but one the wind has found. 'Neither is to blame for being fire. Both should know where the dry grass is.'

A list of the roads' customs, older than any town's laws: share water at a spring, never camp across a path, and a traveller met at dusk is offered the fire before they are asked their name. Scratched beside it: 'And still people ask the name first.'

Before pennies, the records say, trade went by 'the weight of a day's hunting': a hare, two hares, a stag's quarter. A scribe has tried to work out what a penny is in hares and given up at the margin with the note, 'It depends on the hare.'

A song collector's page: every town has a howl for gathering, a howl for warning and a howl for the dead, and no two towns agree which is which. 'This has caused,' the collector writes, 'a number of very short funerals and one very long party.'

On names: in the oldest records a wolf's true name is never written, only what others called it ('the grey one by the ford', 'the one who sings badly'). A later clerk explains that a written name can be read by anyone, and anyone is more people than one wants.

Records of the hard winters, from every town, all ending the same way: who shared, and who did not. The second list is always shorter. The scholar who gathered them notes that the second list is also always written in a smaller hand.

On the first Chapters: bands of wolves who were not kin but chose each other, and wrote their choosing down so no one could say it was not real. The oldest such charter is three lines long. The third line is: 'And we will fight about the rest later.'

A hunter's book of the country between the towns: where the deer cross, where the boar root, where the ground goes soft without warning. Every page has a corner folded down. The last page says only: 'The wild changes. Fold your own corners.'
